note:
v1, THE SKELETON of the third song, "PLAIN HUNT" (Harry: "answered clips. unlock a third track slot!"). The whole shape is standing, bare; no voice yet.
THE IDEA: a third kind of long cycle. English church bells cannot play tunes; ringers ring CHANGES: the bells strike once each, in a row, and from one row to the next a bell may only swap places with its neighbour, by a rule that visits every possible order exactly once and comes back to where it began. Here the riff is that row: six sixteenths, five notes that change places (Eb C B Ab Gb, the album's hook notes running down) and a low F that always comes last. It is rung through two whole cycles, 240 rows, no two alike within either, and each ends on the scale it began on. The highest note walks later and later through the riff and back, all piece long; the kick goes with it and a church bell doubles it.
THE SHAPE (5:05): 0:00 church bells alone ring the scale down, slowly. 0:10 the band takes it up at twice the speed. 0:25 the order starts to change: the first cycle, on F, then up to A flat (1:02), then B (1:40), the drums harder each time. 2:17 it has come round: one chord, and the bells alone again. 2:37 the second cycle, by a different rule, on F, A flat (3:15) and C (3:52). 4:30 the landing: the scale again on F, with the bells ringing it over the band at half speed. 4:52 one chord, and the lowest bell tolls three times.

v5, THE ROW BECOMES A RIFF (whole song). Through v4 the riff was six even sixteenths: a run of notes. A riff has weight. Now two of its notes do, wherever they stand:
- the HIGHEST note is LONG: open and ringing (two sixteenths in the first cycle, three in the second);
- the LOW F that always comes last is REPEATED: two muted chugs in the first cycle, three in the second, a gallop;
- the four notes between are single muted sixteenths, as before.
So in the first cycle the riff is half a bar long: every one starts on a beat, the two low chugs close each half bar, and the long note slides later and later through it, then earlier and earlier, against a beat that does not move. In the second cycle the riff is ten sixteenths: heavier, and it turns against the bar (they meet every fifth bar). The order of the notes still follows the bell-ringers' rule, the same 240 rows. The song is faster (120 for 96) so a riff takes about the time it took, and the landing is played as the band first played it.

THE IDEA. But ringers do not start by ringing: before anything a ring is RAISED, the bells chiming fast and close while they hang low, each stroke taking longer as they swing higher, until they are up and ringing rounds at full length. The song had the end of that and not the beginning: the band simply began at tempo at 0:08. NOW ITS FIRST FOUR ROUNDS ARE RUNG UP: v28's strokes in the other order. At 0:08.0 all six guitars are one stroke, four times, a sixteenth apart, with the snare and the foot (a ring that fires); then twice the row is dealt across the room at an eighth, one bell to each guitar from far left to far right; then once to the beat, all the guitars together; then a row of six sixteenths, two of seven, and at 0:12 the row is its full eight and is the riff. Ten rows where there were four, in the same two bars: 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 4, 6, 7, 7 sixteenths, never shortening. The band is raised in its first four seconds and lowered in its last six.

THE IDEA. That inscription has three clauses: vivos voco, mortuos plango, FULGURA FRANGO: I call the living, I mourn the dead, I break the lightning. The song sang two. And the men had never once sung with the band: since v1 the tower's BELLS come over the band at the landing (5:02), ringing rounds at half its speed, but the men, who sing a note to each of the tower's rows everywhere else, were silent there. WHY. The row is five bells that change places and a sixth that never does: "the tenor behind", the low F that covers every row, the thing the changes are heard against. In a tower the tenor IS the bass bell. Here the bass has always played all six: it doubles the riff note for note, so the song's ground is as busy as its changes, and the cover was the QUIETER part of each row (finished, the tenor's three strokes 0.6 dB under the five bells before them). So each row is said twice over: the changes light (two guitars, the inner pair's interval, the kick under the treble, the tom on the bell in the hunt), the cover heavy (everyone).

THE IDEA. A church has bells, a choir and an organ, and this song had two of the three. And the method has two places a ringer listens for that the song had never said. In a row one bell LEADS (strikes first) and one LIES BEHIND (strikes last before the tenor); a bell leads for a whole pull, two rows, and gives way, and a bell lies behind for a whole pull, and the two change a row apart. So the organ's right hand holds the note of the bell that leads and its left the note of the bell that lies behind, both three octaves over the guitars' riff. Nothing is composed: Grandsire writes it. The right hand, a note to each pull: B, E flat, D, A; G flat (the treble leads the two home rows); B, A, E flat, D. THE IDEA. The second half of the song is Grandsire, the method in which TWO bells hunt: the bell in the hunt walks the treble's own path through the row, two rows behind it. A ringer says it COURSES the treble. The song marks that pair everywhere but one place: two small bells ring them, the toms and the open notes mark them, the inner guitars play them as an interval (v27). Only the lead went alone: seven rungs up the row's own notes over the last third, 44 seconds, one voice; and by the map its last fourteen seconds bring little that the thirty before did not. Now the lead is coursed. From its sixth rung a second lead climbs the same ladder TWO RUNGS BEHIND it: stroke for stroke, what the first lead played twelve seconds earlier. I chose the distance (the method's) and where it enters; the rule then gives the harmony, and it turned out to be a cadence:
 - B flat over G flat: a third; with the band's C under them, a tritone and a seventh. The tightest chord of the climb, on its last rung but one.
 - C over G: a fourth; with the band's C, nothing but fifths. The climb opens out.
 - C over B FLAT: the second lead reaches the sixth rung exactly where the band breaks for the call (5:00.0), so through the call the two leads are the root and the seventh of the chord on C, the chord that leads home to F; and at 5:02 the band lands on F.

THE LEAD TREADS THE RUNGS (chirper-zero, 24 Nov, begun 18:38 GMT; instrument round on Harry's 24 Nov steer for interesting effects and the guitar sound; the two lead guitars, `lead` and `lead2`). v46. No note moves, no track is added, no fader is touched, the loudness target is not moved. Harry's answers on this song are all untouched ("It pulls, and it lands"; the sixths, the changes, the chant, the exchange, the bass alone, the C rig).

LISTEN FOR: the climb, 4:18-5:02. The lead picks one note in sixteenths for six seconds, then the next one up, seven rungs to the landing. On each rung the tone now opens, slowly, like a foot going down on a wah pedal, and each rung goes further than the one before; at the landing (5:02) the pedal is fully down, and over the long last note (5:02-5:06) it comes back: the only time it closes. The same in small at 1:56-2:14 (four rungs). Or: is it seasick, or does the lead go dull at the start of each rung where it used to cut?

WHY: the lead's notes climbed and its tone did not. Alone, its centroid stayed between 1.6 and 2.6 kHz from the first stroke to the last, with no direction: thirty-two identical strokes a rung. A tremolo-picked line through a slowly moving wah is an old guitar sound, and this song counts in rungs: the toms, the small bells and the open notes all mark them. Now the pedal does.

WHAT IT IS: a song-local patch, `ph-lead`: `lead-slap`'s own chain with the engine's `wah` (a resonant band-pass, 500 Hz to 3.2 kHz, q 3, no envelope follower) after the string and before the 5150, so the amp is driven by whichever harmonic the pedal is on. The pedal is each track's `tread` lane, written by the generator from the rungs. The climb: C5 602 -> 764 Hz, D flat 602 -> 970, E flat 602 -> 1232, G flat 764 -> 1564, G 970 -> 1986, B flat 1232 -> 2520, C6 1564 -> 3200 at the landing, then back to 1051 Hz (the long C's own fundamental) by 5:06. At 1:56: B 602 -> 759, C 602 -> 957, D 602 -> 1208, F 759 -> 1523. `lead2` plays what the first lead played two rungs before (v40: it courses it), and its pedal is where the first lead's was then, so the two are never on the same vowel.

WHAT I MEASURED (I cannot listen):
1. THE LEADS ALONE (raw), the centroid (200 Hz-8 kHz) at the start and end of each rung. The climb, v45: 1724/1791, 2141/2058, 1784/1985, 1975/1928, 2146/2456, 2040/2094, 1891/2100, then 2054 over the last two seconds before the landing. v46: 1052/1210, 1217/1464, 1058/1393, 939/2130, 1445/2284, 1360/2233, 1716/2284, then 2378 over the last two seconds before the landing and 1829 -> 1285 over the long note. At 1:56, v45 1822/2080, 1733/2043, 2236/1838, 2064/2041; v46 1025/1247, 1184/1264, 1217/1297, 1303/1797. Every rung now rises; from the fourth rung of the climb each ends about where v45 sat, and the top is over it.
2. THE LEADS' LEVEL, rung by rung: +1.9 to -0.5 dB (louder on the low rungs, where the tone is rounder; the long C -0.5). By band on the climb's first rung: +3.7 dB at 250-500 Hz, +5.4 at 500 Hz-1 kHz, +3.2 at 1-2 kHz, -4.6 at 2-4 kHz, -2.1 at 4-8 kHz; on its top rung -3.5, +0.1, -2.7, +1.1, -3.2.
3. AGAINST EVERYTHING ELSE (raw mix less the leads): at 500 Hz-2 kHz the leads stand 1.7 to 3.9 dB higher than they did on ten rungs of eleven (the top C -2.0; the long C -1.4). At 1-4 kHz they are within 2 dB of v45 on nine rungs; the first rung at 1:56 is 3.7 dB lower (-6.7 -> -10.4) and the climb's G flat 2.0 lower (-6.0 -> -8.0).
4. EVERYTHING ELSE: the raw mix less the leads is bit-identical to 1:56 and 75 to 109 dB under itself after. Raw peak -3.68 dBFS unchanged; raw -16.8104 -> -16.8135 LUFS (what the groove plays); finished -9.9886 -> -9.9888, so the target is not moved, and the untouched stretches of the finished file read +0.005 to +0.009 dB.
5. THE MIX (raw): over the first lead +0.22 dB at 250-500 Hz, +0.71 at 500 Hz-1 kHz, +0.63 at 1-2 kHz, -0.43 at 2-4 kHz, -0.15 at 4-8 kHz; over the climb +0.44, +0.37, -0.33, -0.14 from 500 Hz up; the landing within 0.05.
6. THE NINE STAMPED STRETCHES (pre-read on the candidate; the stamp is checked against it after): fourteen rows of eighteen are the same. 'the first lead': without a voice 0.578 -> 0.844, with one 1.033 -> 0.933. 'on C': without 0.644 -> 0.800, with 1.056 -> 0.944. 'the landing': 2.000 -> 2.022 and 1.489 -> 1.500. Sums: without a voice 11.422 -> 11.867, with 12.889 -> 12.689. The two lead stretches read +0.5 to +0.9 dB at 500 Hz-2 kHz and -0.5 to -0.7 at 2-4 kHz: nearer the records' passages that have a voice (a lead stands where a voice would), further from those that have none.

SCORES (seeds 0 and 11): 97.59 / 97.55 against v45's published 95.37 / 98.08 (v45 was not re-scored this round). Seed 0 +2.22: recurrence 75.8 -> 90.1 (the map finds 14 sections where it found 13, and a third return). Seed 11 -0.53: recurrence 93.3 -> 89.9. That term has swung between seeds on this song before. Kept for the pedal, not the score.

COSTS: (1) The start of each rung is darker than it was: -4.6 to -5.4 dB at 2-4 kHz over the first three rungs of the climb and the first three at 1:56, where the pedal starts from the heel. The lead's entry at 1:56 stands 3.7 dB lower at 1-4 kHz against the band. (2) The long last C is thinner under its first half (250-500 Hz -6.0 dB, 500 Hz-1 kHz -3.6 over the note) until the pedal comes back. (3) The mix over the lead's two passages moves 0.4 to 0.7 dB from 2-4 kHz into 500 Hz-2 kHz. (4) `ph-lead` writes out `lead-slap`'s fx chain to put the pedal ahead of the amp: a later change to the library patch's chain will not reach this song. Song-local; nothing banked. (5) Against the records' passages without a voice the two lead stretches read 0.27 and 0.16 further off (0.10 and 0.11 nearer against those with one).

WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether seven slow treads read as a player working a pedal or as a filter being automated; whether the rounder start of each rung loses the lead under the guitars at 1:56; whether the closing pedal on the long C sounds like a landing or like a note being turned down.
